title: When 5,000 formations changed the simulation architecture
body:
the 5,000-formation Scenario Lab started as a scale test. it ended up showing where the current ownership model stopped making sense.

on the M1 baseline, the moving workload was around 123.4 ms per tick. it was not one bad loop. the same dynamic formation state was getting prepared, crossed, traversed, and republished through planning, movement, targeting, history, and presentation.

so the high-volume active state moved into one dense C++ owner. formations still keep their identities, orders, positions, health, targets, and deterministic consequences. commands still enter on the tick boundary, results still commit in stable order, and the GDScript reference fixtures stay there for parity.

the matched local headless 5,000-formation moving workload is now around 0.993 ms per tick on that same M1. that is simulation time for this build and workload, not a general capacity claim, rendering benchmark, or proof of the video’s frame pacing.

the clip is just the scenarios running: 2v2, 50v50 line versus column, then a separate 2,500v2,500 native-core battle.

the useful result is not “C++ good, GDScript bad.” the prototype made the behavior easy to explore. the scale test showed that the ownership boundary itself needed to change.

videos.caption: Visual composition/progression evidence only: separate 2v2 (4s), 50v50 line-versus-column (6s), and 2,500v2,500 native-core (8s) Scenario Labs. This muted fixed-offline clip does not prove the benchmark or interactive frame pacing.
